name: Triangle Choke from Crackhead Control
summary: The triangle choke from Crackhead Control is a 10th Planet rubber guard blood choke that uses the shin already pinned across the opponent's face as a guide rail to shoot the choking leg over the far shoulder, compressing both carotid arteries with minimal transition distance.
description: Complete guide to the triangle choke from Crackhead Control. Master the 10th Planet setup, finishing mechanics, counters, and defensive escape strategies.
overview:
The triangle choke from Crackhead Control is one of the highest-percentage submissions available from the 10th Planet rubber guard system. Crackhead Control positions the bottom player's shin across the opponent's face and neck, creating a posture-breaking framework that naturally sets up triangle choke entries. Because the attacking leg is already at neck level and the opponent's posture is compromised, the transition to a locked triangle requires fewer steps than traditional closed guard setups, giving the defender significantly less time to mount an effective defense.

The position's strength lies in the asymmetric control it creates. The shin pressing across the opponent's face serves as both a barrier to posture recovery and a guide rail for the choking leg. By isolating one arm and swimming the locking leg over the far shoulder, the bottom player can establish the triangle configuration without the typical struggle of elevating hips and climbing legs that characterizes standard guard triangle attempts. This reduced transition distance means the opponent has fewer defensive windows to prevent the lock from closing.

Strategically, the triangle from Crackhead Control functions as a primary threat within the rubber guard attacking system. It chains naturally with gogoplata, omoplata, and armbar attacks, creating a submission web where defending one threat exposes the opponent to another. The position is particularly effective in no-gi grappling where the absence of collar grips makes traditional posture-breaking more difficult, and Crackhead Control's mechanical posture break compensates for this limitation.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate upon release, but potential for injury if held after tap

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain or cervical spine stress
Brachial plexus compression causing temporary arm numbness

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow partner to tap. NEVER spike or jerk the finish.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any distress sound)
Physical hand tap (multiple taps on body or mat)
Any loss of resistance or going limp
release_protocol: Immediately open legs and release triangle configuration
Remove shin from neck and lower legs to mat
Release arm trap and create space
If unconscious, place in recovery position and alert instructor
training_restrictions: NEVER hold triangle after tap or loss of consciousness
NEVER use competition finishing speed in training
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with at least one hand
Release immediately upon any tap signal
Monitor partner's color and breathing throughout
Practice finishing mechanics on cooperative partners first

attacker.name: from Crackhead Control Attacker
attacker.description: Step-by-step guide to attacking the triangle choke from Crackhead Control. Setup mechanics, finishing details, and counter responses for serious grapplers.
attacker.overview: Attacking the triangle choke from Crackhead Control leverages the rubber guard system's inherent posture-breaking mechanics to create a short-distance triangle entry. The shin already positioned across the opponent's face provides a natural framework for the choking leg, while the broken posture eliminates the most common defensive response. Success depends on proper arm isolation, smooth leg transition, and committed angle adjustment before applying the squeeze. The compressed distance between Crackhead Control and the locked triangle gives the attacker a significant timing advantage over standard closed guard triangle setups, reducing defensive windows from multiple distinct steps to essentially one critical transition moment.
key_principles: Maintain complete posture control throughout the transition from Crackhead Control to locked triangle, never releasing head control during leg movement
Isolate the far arm across your centerline before initiating the triangle leg transition, as both arms inside the triangle creates a structurally weak choke
Use the shin across the face as a guide rail for the choking leg, transitioning smoothly from face control to neck compression
Cut the angle 30 degrees toward the trapped arm side immediately after locking to create proper bilateral carotid compression
Elevate hips off the mat during the finish to generate upward pressure that compounds the leg squeeze
Treat the triangle from Crackhead Control as part of a submission chain, threatening gogoplata and omoplata to create defensive dilemmas
setup_requirements: Crackhead Control fully established with shin across opponent's face and posture completely broken, forehead near your chest
Head control secured with at least one hand cupping the back of the opponent's head to prevent posture recovery during transition
Far arm isolated across your centerline, confirmed past your midline before beginning triangle leg transition
Hips mobile and positioned to angle off once the triangle lock closes, not flat on the mat
Opponent's base compromised through broken posture so they cannot generate explosive posture recovery during the transition window

execution_steps.description: From closed guard, walk your shin across the opponent's face while cupping the back of their head with your controlling hand. Break their posture completely until their forehead is near your chest, establishing the mechanical foundation for the triangle entry with your leg already at neck height.

Use your free hand to push the opponent's far arm across your centerline, directing it between your bodies. Confirm the arm is past your midline before proceeding. This arm isolation determines the choking side and is the single most critical setup element for finishing effectiveness.

execution_steps.action: Shoot the locking leg over the shoulder
execution_steps.description: Release the shin from across their face and immediately shoot that leg over their far shoulder on the trapped-arm side. The shin that was controlling their face transitions directly to the choking position across the back of their neck. Maintain head control with your hands throughout this brief but critical transition window.

Bring your opposite leg up and secure the triangle by placing the back of your choking leg's knee over the ankle or shin of your bottom leg. Squeeze your knees together to close the initial lock, trapping the opponent's arm and head inside the triangle configuration and eliminating their primary escape routes.

execution_steps.action: Cut the angle toward the trapped arm
execution_steps.description: Pivot your hips approximately 30 degrees toward the side of the trapped arm. This angular adjustment creates perpendicular alignment between your legs and the opponent's neck, which is essential for proper bilateral carotid compression rather than an ineffective frontal squeeze that only causes discomfort.

Pull the opponent's head down with both hands clasped behind their neck while squeezing your thighs together. Elevate your hips slightly off the mat to increase upward pressure on the carotid arteries. Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum to allow adequate time for your partner to recognize the choke and tap.

If the choke does not finish within 10 seconds, make targeted micro-adjustments: verify the trapped arm is fully across your centerline, increase the hip angle, underhook the far leg to prevent stacking defense, or overhook your own shin to pull the choking leg deeper across the back of the neck.

common_counters.counter: Explosive posture recovery before triangle lock closes
common_counters.your_response: Maintain head control with both hands during the leg transition and immediately re-establish Crackhead Control if posture recovers. Use the brief forward momentum of their posture attempt to shoot the locking leg over their shoulder.

common_counters.counter: Stack defense driving forward to change the choking angle
common_counters.your_response: Underhook their far thigh with your hand to block forward drive, or scoot hips away to maintain the perpendicular angle. If the stack succeeds, transition to armbar on the trapped arm rather than fighting the compressed position.

common_counters.counter: Arm extraction by rotating the trapped arm toward the lock opening
common_counters.your_response: Squeeze knees tighter and pull the head down to compress space around the trapped arm. If extraction begins, immediately overhook the arm with your hand to re-secure it, or transition to omoplata on the escaping arm.

common_errors.error: Failing to angle off after locking the triangle
common_errors.consequence: Creates a frontal compression that is primarily muscular and does not efficiently target the carotid arteries, resulting in a tiring squeeze the opponent can survive through good posture defense
common_errors.correction: Pivot hips 30 degrees toward the trapped arm side immediately after closing the lock, creating perpendicular alignment between your legs and the opponent's neck for proper bilateral compression

common_errors.error: Rushing the leg transition without maintaining head control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent postures up during the brief transition window when the shin leaves their face, escaping Crackhead Control entirely and negating the setup
common_errors.correction: Keep at least one hand cupping the back of the head throughout the leg transition. Release the shin only when your pulling hand has firm downward control of the head

common_errors.error: Attempting the triangle without first isolating the far arm
common_errors.consequence: Both arms remain inside the triangle giving the opponent strong framing ability, posture recovery options, and the structural space to prevent proper carotid compression
common_errors.correction: Always confirm one arm is across your centerline before beginning the triangle transition. The arm isolation is the single most critical prerequisite for a finishing triangle

common_errors.error: Locking the triangle with incorrect leg configuration
common_errors.consequence: The choking leg ends up on the wrong side of the neck, creating an ineffective squeeze that compresses the trachea rather than the carotid arteries
common_errors.correction: The leg that was across the face becomes the choking leg across the back of the neck, with the other leg locking underneath by placing the knee pit over the shin

common_errors.error: Keeping hips flat on the mat during the finishing squeeze
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient hip elevation means less upward pressure on the carotid arteries, resulting in a loose choke the opponent can survive or escape through patient defense
common_errors.correction: Elevate hips off the mat while squeezing, creating upward pressure that compounds the thigh compression and tightens the triangle from below

common_errors.error: Squeezing with legs only without controlling the head
common_errors.consequence: The opponent creates enough space through neck extension to relieve carotid pressure, even within a locked triangle configuration
common_errors.correction: Pull the head down with both hands clasped behind the neck or overhook the choking leg shin while squeezing to create compound downward-and-inward pressure

training_progressions.focus: Triangle lock technique from Crackhead Control
training_progressions.description: Practice the leg transition from Crackhead Control to triangle lock on a cooperative partner. Focus on smooth shin-to-neck transition, proper leg locking sequence, and angle adjustment. Perform 50 repetitions per side with no resistance to build clean movement patterns.

Work the full sequence from Crackhead Control establishment through arm isolation to locked triangle. Partner provides light posture resistance to develop timing for the arm push and leg transition. Focus on maintaining head control throughout the entire chain.

From a locked triangle position, practice finishing details including angle optimization, hip elevation, head control, and incremental adjustments against moderate resistance. Partner attempts basic escapes including posture recovery and stacking to test finishing effectiveness.

Incorporate the triangle from Crackhead Control into positional sparring rounds starting from closed guard. Work the full chain from guard entry to Crackhead Control to triangle attempt against fully resisting opponents. Track attempt and finish rates to identify areas for refinement.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the triangle choke from Crackhead Control primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The triangle choke compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously using the thigh on one side and the opponent's own trapped shoulder on the other. The choking leg presses against one carotid while the squeezing action drives the opponent's shoulder into the opposite carotid. This bilateral carotid compression restricts blood flow to the brain, causing unconsciousness within approximately 8-12 seconds of proper application.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the triangle is properly locked and the opponent is approaching the breaking point?
flashcards.answer: Key indicators include the opponent's face changing color through reddening or flushing, decreased resistance in their escape attempts, involuntary reaching or flailing movements, and progressive weakening of posture recovery efforts. The attacker should also feel the squeeze tightening as the opponent's trapped shoulder drives deeper into their own neck. If these signs are absent after 5-7 seconds, the angle or lock likely needs adjustment.

flashcards.question: What control must be established before transitioning from Crackhead Control to the triangle attempt?
flashcards.answer: Before initiating the triangle transition, you must have broken posture with the opponent's forehead near your chest, secure head control with at least one hand cupping the back of the head, the far arm isolated across your centerline, and your shin firmly pressed across the opponent's face. The arm isolation is the most critical prerequisite because attempting the triangle with both arms inside gives the opponent strong framing and posture recovery options.

flashcards.question: At what point during the triangle from Crackhead Control is the opponent past the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The point of no return occurs when the triangle is locked with proper angle and the opponent's trapped arm is fully across the centerline. Once the angle is cut to approximately 30 degrees toward the trapped arm side and the lock is tight, defensive options become extremely limited. Before the lock closes, the opponent has multiple defensive windows. After the lock but before the angle, stacking remains viable. Once both conditions are met, only explosive posture recovery offers realistic escape.

flashcards.question: What is the most common finishing error when applying the triangle from Crackhead Control?
flashcards.answer: The most common finishing error is failing to angle off after locking the triangle. Many practitioners squeeze straight on, creating compression that is primarily muscular and does not efficiently target the carotid arteries. Without the 30-degree angle toward the trapped arm, the choking leg and shoulder do not create precise bilateral compression. This results in a tiring squeeze the opponent can often survive through patient posture defense and gradual space creation.

flashcards.question: How should you adjust your grips during the finishing sequence of the triangle from Crackhead Control?
flashcards.answer: During the finish, transition from the head control grip used during setup to pulling the opponent's head down with both hands clasped behind their neck. If the opponent's posture resistance is strong, switch one hand to underhook their far thigh to block stacking defense. For maximum compression, overhook the choking leg's shin with both hands and pull it deeper across the neck. Grip priority shifts from positional control during setup to compression assistance during the finish.

flashcards.question: What are the primary safety concerns when applying the triangle choke from Crackhead Control in training?
flashcards.answer: The primary safety concern is the rapid onset of blood choke effects, with unconsciousness possible within 8-12 seconds of proper application. Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum to give your partner adequate time to recognize the choke and tap. Never jerk or spike the squeeze. Monitor your partner's responsiveness throughout and release immediately upon any tap signal. The transition from uncomfortable pressure to unconsciousness can be rapid once the angle and lock are properly set.

flashcards.question: How should you release the triangle choke from Crackhead Control after a tap?
flashcards.answer: Upon receiving any tap signal, immediately open your legs and release the triangle configuration. Remove your shin from the neck and lower both legs to the mat. Release the arm trap and create space for your partner to recover. Check their consciousness and breathing before continuing. If your partner is unresponsive or went limp before tapping, place them in recovery position and immediately alert the instructor. Never hold the position while debating whether a movement was a tap.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins stacking you after the triangle is locked - what adjustment prevents them from escaping?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent stacks forward, underhook their far thigh with your hand to block forward drive, or scoot your hips away from their pressure to maintain the perpendicular choking angle. The stack can actually tighten the choke if you maintain angle, since the forward pressure drives their shoulder deeper into their own carotid. If they stack successfully despite your adjustments, transition to armbar on the trapped arm rather than exhausting yourself fighting the compressed position.

flashcards.question: How does the triangle setup from Crackhead Control differ from a standard closed guard triangle and why is this advantageous?
flashcards.answer: From standard closed guard, the triangle requires breaking posture, climbing hips high, isolating an arm, and shooting a leg over the shoulder, with each step offering a defensive window. From Crackhead Control, the posture is already broken, the leg is already at neck height via the shin across the face, and arm isolation is often already established. This dramatically shortens the transition distance, reducing defensive opportunities from four distinct windows to essentially one critical moment when the shin transitions from face control to neck choke.

defender.name: from Crackhead Control Defender
defender.description: How to defend and escape the triangle choke from Crackhead Control. Recognition cues, posture recovery techniques, and proven escape strategies for all levels.
defender.overview: Defending the triangle choke from Crackhead Control requires early recognition of the attacking sequence and immediate posture recovery before the triangle lock closes. The compressed distance between Crackhead Control and the locked triangle means defensive windows are narrow, making prevention significantly more effective than late-stage escape attempts. Understanding the attacker's grip sequence and leg positioning provides critical early warning signals that enable timely defensive responses. Once the triangle is fully locked with proper angle, escape percentages drop dramatically, so the defender must commit to prevention-first defense and react to the earliest recognition cues rather than waiting to confirm the attack.
key_principles: Defend the arm isolation above all else because both arms inside the triangle provides strong defensive structure while one arm across creates a finishing position
Recover posture the instant the shin begins to leave your face, as this brief transition window is the widest defensive opportunity available
Stack forward rather than pull backward when caught in the triangle, since pulling away creates space for the attacker to improve angle and tighten the lock
Keep your trapped arm tight to your body rather than reaching or flailing, which only helps the attacker complete the choke configuration
Maintain awareness of the attacker's hip angle because a straight-on triangle is survivable while an angled triangle compresses the carotids efficiently
Tap early and without hesitation when bilateral carotid pressure is established, as the window between discomfort and unconsciousness is narrow with blood chokes
recognition_cues: The opponent's shin pressing across your face begins to lighten or shift upward, indicating they are preparing to transition it from face control to the choking leg position across the back of your neck
Your far arm is being actively pushed or pulled across the opponent's centerline while in Crackhead Control, which is the critical arm isolation step before the triangle attempt
The opponent's hips begin to angle or pivot while maintaining strong head control, indicating preparation for the triangle lock and angle adjustment
You feel the opponent's free hand transition from general posture control to specifically cupping the back of your head with strong downward pulling pressure

defensive_options.action: Explosive posture recovery before the triangle lock closes
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon recognizing the shin leaving your face or feeling the leg shoot over your shoulder, before the lock is secured
defensive_options.if_successful: Return to Crackhead Control top position with posture intact and triangle attempt neutralized
defensive_options.risk: Opponent may transition to gogoplata or omoplata if you posture without simultaneously defending the arm trap

defensive_options.action: Stack defense by driving forward and walking around to change the choking angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the triangle is locked but before the attacker has fully cut the angle, when you still have base and forward drive available
defensive_options.if_successful: Change the triangle angle enough to relieve carotid pressure and eventually pass through to closed guard top or side control
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker maintains the angle during your stack, the forward pressure can drive your own shoulder deeper into your carotid and tighten the choke

defensive_options.action: Arm extraction by rotating the trapped arm toward the lock opening
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the triangle is locked when posture recovery has failed and stacking is not viable due to attacker controlling your thigh
defensive_options.if_successful: Both arms inside the triangle creates defensive structure that prevents the finish and allows gradual posture recovery
defensive_options.risk: Opponent may transition to armbar on the extracting arm during the rotation movement

escape_paths: Posture recovery through framing on opponent's hips and driving upward before the triangle lock closes, returning to Crackhead Control top
Stack defense by driving forward and walking to the side to change the choking angle, eventually extracting head and arm to pass to top position
Arm extraction by rotating the trapped arm toward the lock opening while posting the other hand for base and posture

favorable_outcomes.how: Stack through the triangle by driving forward with proper posture while walking around to the side to progressively change the choking angle, then extract your head and arm to establish top position in closed guard

common_errors.error: Pulling away from the triangle instead of driving forward into the stack
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for the attacker to improve their angle, tighten the squeeze, and elevate hips, converting a survivable position into a finishing one
common_errors.correction: Drive forward and stack rather than pulling backward. Forward pressure can neutralize the angle while backward movement gives the attacker exactly the space they need

common_errors.error: Reaching with the free arm to push on the opponent's choking leg
common_errors.consequence: Overextended arm provides armbar opportunity and reduces base stability, while rarely generating enough force to open a properly locked triangle
common_errors.correction: Keep the free arm tight and use body positioning, posture, and angle changes rather than arm pushing. Post the free hand on the mat for base during stack defense

common_errors.error: Allowing both arms to be trapped inside the triangle during setup
common_errors.consequence: Opponent has complete arm control with both arms inside, making any defensive movement extremely difficult and giving the attacker a structurally sound finishing position
common_errors.correction: Defend the arm isolation aggressively from Crackhead Control. Keep at least one arm outside the triangle configuration by fighting the arm push early before the leg transition begins

common_errors.error: Panicking and thrashing when the triangle locks instead of executing systematic defense
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy rapidly and often tightens the choke by creating movement that the attacker exploits for angle and compression adjustments
common_errors.correction: Stay calm, assess the lock quality and angle, then execute systematic escape steps in priority order: posture recovery, stack with angle walk, arm extraction

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the triangle choke from Crackhead Control is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cues are the opponent's shin across your face beginning to shift or lighten as they prepare to transition it to a choking position, your far arm being actively pushed across their centerline, and increased head-pulling pressure from the controlling hand. The most urgent combined signal is arm isolation plus the shin leaving your face, indicating the triangle transition is imminent and you have approximately 1-2 seconds to mount an effective defense.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the triangle choke from Crackhead Control?
flashcards.answer: Tap clearly and immediately when you feel bilateral pressure on both sides of your neck or any lightheadedness. Use multiple rapid taps on your opponent's body or the mat with your free hand. If your hands are trapped, tap with your feet or verbally say tap. Do not wait to see if you can tough it out or escape. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness within 8-12 seconds of proper application, and the window between uncomfortable pressure and loss of consciousness is deceptively narrow.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the triangle choke from Crackhead Control?
flashcards.answer: Three primary defenses in order of effectiveness: first, early posture recovery before the lock closes by framing on the opponent's hips and driving upward while defending arm isolation. Second, stacking defense by driving forward after the lock closes but before the angle is fully cut, walking around to the side to change the choking geometry. Third, arm extraction by rotating the trapped arm toward the lock opening while maintaining base. Prevention through early posture recovery is significantly more effective than any late-stage escape.

flashcards.question: Why is stacking sometimes counterproductive when defending the triangle from Crackhead Control?
flashcards.answer: Stacking can be counterproductive because if the attacker maintains proper angle during the stack, the forward driving pressure actually pushes your own trapped shoulder deeper into your carotid artery, tightening the choke rather than relieving it. Effective stacking requires simultaneously changing the angle by walking to the side rather than driving straight forward. Additionally, stacking without addressing the arm trap leaves you vulnerable to the attacker switching to an armbar on the trapped arm from the compressed position.

training_progressions.description: Partner works Crackhead Control entries and triangle setups at half speed. Defender practices identifying the three key recognition cues: shin shifting, arm isolation attempts, and head control changes. Call out each cue as recognized to build conscious awareness before developing physical responses.

training_progressions.focus: Early posture recovery and arm defense
training_progressions.description: Start from Crackhead Control with partner attempting triangle setups at progressively increasing speed. Focus exclusively on maintaining posture and preventing arm isolation. Track the percentage of attempts where you successfully prevent the triangle lock from closing.

training_progressions.focus: Stack defense and arm extraction techniques
training_progressions.description: Start from a locked triangle position with varying levels of angle. Practice stack defense with angle walking and arm extraction techniques against moderate then full resistance. Develop muscle memory for systematic escape sequences under realistic pressure.

Positional sparring starting from Crackhead Control. Partner works full-speed triangle attempts while defender applies all defensive tools from recognition through prevention to escape. Integrate all phases into fluid defensive responses under competition-level intensity.
